This is the sort of thing that gets really easily twisted to suit an agenda. How much does it take to say, "Look, people can't concentrate on anything anymore because of the web!"

But if you go and look at just how much information is flung at us in the modern world, we expect to see most sources of information quickly checked to see if they're worth spending more time on. Your brain already does this on a subconscious level with all of the sensory data it receives: We can't possibly pay attention to every single stimulus, so the brain culls anything that isn't interesting enough to be worth the effort of examining closer.

"Average webpage attention" statistics are in the same category as "average pixel attention" statistics. If we saw a number that was much higher than these results, that would be bad because it represents difficulty culling insignificant stimulus. IIRC, this is what a lot of people with ADHD experience (subjectively, at least. I don't know if objective tests bear it out.)

I thought it was more the sudden and seemingly random absorption with inappropriate objects at the expense of others. For example, suddenly counting the number of poles in a distant fence in the middle of a conversation. It probably manifests in different ways per person though.

Well, I guess I have to come clean and confess that I do have ADHD and what I described is how I experience it myself. I put the IIRC in because I don't remember for sure how common it is, but I'm led to believe it's quite common indeed.

Jumping topics in a conversation is a common example of ADHD behavior, but I think it's not particularly illustrative of the point I was trying to make. A better example might be trying to hold a conversation in a noisy environment like a restaurant. A normal person is able to ignore the noises of conversations at other tables, clinking of dishes, maybe a noisy coffee maker, whatever.

I do that very poorly: If something is loud enough for me to notice, it's on my mind. I'll be thinking about how a waiter moves, or why different dishes sound the way they do when they hit things just as much as I think about the topic of conversation. These are the kinds of stimuli that need to be filtered out before someone can actually "pay attention" to an important thing, which is why I strongly believe that the statistics quoted in the page OP linked are misleading.

This is exactly why writing clickbait is so effective. People read the headline, skim the article, ignore it, and move on. I think it's some sort of feedback loop where this kind of content makes people less attentive and less serious, and the worse they get, the more they seek out this type of content.

We're not learning less, we're offloading unnecessary information storage to our computers. If I have to go to a library to get a book to learn about penguins I'm paying a high opportunity cost, so it makes sense to really study that book. If I can get any common penguin knowledge in a fifteen second web search I don't need to study that penguin page. I can skip to the one data point I need at the moment and move on. This is a very poor -- useless even -- measure of cognitive ability.
